title: the breath again — every claim checked
hook: in the Gita's list of offerings, some people offer their breath, and it sits in a row with everyone else's gift
carry: the breath again — every claim checked

segments.voice: Yesterday, the breath again: a yoga manual said breath is tamed like a lion, slowly. Its caution stayed, and its promise got checked.

What would it mean to give a breath away? Not to hold it, or push it, or count it. To offer it, the way a person sets a flower down in front of an image or pours a spoon of ghee into a fire. In the fourth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna walks Arjuna through a long list of offerings people make. Wealth, study, discipline, the restraint of the senses. And in the middle of the list, quietly, breath. Today: what the Gita does with the breath, and a claim about it that the list itself answers.
screen: `GIVE A BREATH AWAY?` → `A LIST OF OFFERINGS.` → `BREATH, IN THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in paraphrase. Some, Krishna says, offer the in-breath into the out-breath, and the out-breath into the in-breath, holding the path of both, given over to the practice of breath. The breath going in is poured into the breath going out, like an offering into a fire, and back again. Breathing itself becomes a yajna, a sacrifice. The ordinary thing the body does all day is treated as a gift. Then look at the company it keeps. Some offer their senses into the fire of restraint. Some offer their possessions. Some offer austerity, some study, some yoga. And a short line sums up the whole row: all of these know what sacrifice is. Now the claim. You'll sometimes hear that the Gita names breath control as the highest yoga, the secret above all others. Check it against the chapter. Breath is there, honored, given its own careful verse. But it stands in a row with study, with giving, with self-restraint. The list doesn't crown it. What the Gita adds is a direction: the point of the breath isn't what you get from it, but what you give with it. Later, in the fifth chapter, the Gita mentions making the in-breath and out-breath even as they move within the nostrils, and there too breath serves a larger aim: a person free of desire, fear and anger. So the claim shrinks, and the teaching grows. In the Gita, breath can be an offering.
screen: `IN-BREATH POURED INTO OUT-BREATH` · `BREATHING AS A SACRIFICE` · `ONE GIFT IN A ROW OF GIFTS` · `NOT WHAT YOU GET, BUT WHAT YOU GIVE`

segments.voice: Notice the breath in arriving and let it flow into the breath out without a seam, then the breath out turning into the breath in, like the gentlest offering: something set down, not thrown. If you pray, you can offer your breathing, just as it is, to God, as some Hindus do; if you don't, you can simply let it go with thanks.
The breath again. In the Gita, some offer the in-breath into the out-breath, one gift in a row of many. Today's word.
Your line: the breath again — every claim checked. One ordinary breath, set down as a gift. See you tomorrow.

chat.says: Does the Gita say breath control is the secret above every other practice?
options: No, breath gets its own verse, but it stands in a row with study and giving.
Yes, Krishna crowns it the one offering that all the others serve.
No, the Gita never mentions the breath at all, only wealth and study.
chat.meaning: In Gita 4 breath is one offering among many, beside study, giving and restraint; the list honors it but doesn't crown it.

notes: Gita 4.29: confirm the paraphrase 'offer the in-breath into the out-breath and the out-breath into the in-breath, restraining the course of both, devoted to breath control'. Commentators differ on which of prana/apana is the in-breath; the lesson follows the common reading (prana in, apana out) — a Keeper should confirm or soften.

Gita 4.33 (the offering of knowledge is called superior to material offerings) is deliberately not mentioned; the lesson says only that the list does not crown breath control. Check that this is a fair reading.
Original: pronunciation of yajna varies by region (YUG-nyuh, YUG-yuh, YAJ-nuh).
Practice line 'as some Hindus do' offering breathing to God: confirm this is fair and unforced.
